RUSSIAN OPINIONS UPON THE INDIAN MUTINIES. Shortsighted would those people in Europe be who should wish England to suffer sensible losses in East India. In the present state of industry and commerce England is indispensable for Europe. It is true that she receives great advantages for herself from such a state of things, but at the same time others as well are benefited thereby. To the enterprising spirit of the English Europe is indebted for the development in its centre of manufactures and industry. The example of Eugland, the advantages drawn by her from the working up of raw produce, have shown to others what the present position of civilized European society is in an industrial point of view compared with that of societies which are less civilized and less developed in what relates to industry and commerce. In England, at the present time, that universal steam-machine has taken up its place which puts into movement enormous capital, encourages commercial speculations in all the countries of the world, and thus procures benefits not only to private individuals, but to kingdoms, the revenues of which are increased in proportion as private industry flourishes. To the latter great liberty is given in England, which it cannot obtain for itself yet in the other kingdoms of Europe, and this is the cause of so great a development of the commercial and industrial strength of England. If her strength becomes tottering the other people of Europe feel it also in different degrees. The political relations of England to

Europe and the other parts of the world are another affair. It is indispensable that England should change its form of action. CURRENTS OF THE OCEAN. Oue ot the most important contributions to science that has been made of late years is the work of Lieuteuaut Maury on the Physical Geography of the Sea. So many efforts had been made without success to sound the depths of the ocean, that it hud come to be regarded as impracticable. The observation of the currents that were known to exist in its waters were attended with so many difficulties that they were at best but imperfectly understood The same uncertainty prevailed with regard to the winds ; and Navigation, consequently, was a thing pure routine, of vessel followed vessel over a prescribed track year after year, though, as has since been amply proved, a much more advantageous courso might have bst shaped. The universally appreciated book of Lieutenant Maury lays before the public the result of observations made in nil parts of the globe as to the currents and winds, the temperature of the water, and the result of deep sea soundings, þÿ4 C. ; and by the charts which have been constructed, with the aid of these observations, the navigator is enabled boldly to steer over what to him is wholly an unknown sea. Thus many voyages are much shortened, and very great savings oftentimes effected. The Philadelphia North American , in an article on þÿ Winds and þÿCurrents, adduces some interesting facts, from which we make some liberal extracts. It says ; þÿ By far the best known currents in the world of waters is the Gulf Stream, which lies so immediately in the track of modern Commerce.

It has its origin in the Gulf of Mexico, and fliws out so near to the Florida Keys that its deep blue colour is sometimes distinctly visible from them The line of demarcation between the Gulf Stream and the oolder water which serves lor its bed, is remarkably well þÿdefined so much so that it has been possible to distinguish the instnui at which a vessel enters it. Tile geuer.il course of the stream is first to the north-east þÿ off the coast of the United States þÿ ind then turning to the eastward, at about the southern extremity of the Great Bauks, and continually widening on the surface, it is distributed to the I British Islands and the North of Europe, the natural rigour of whioh it serves greatly to temper. The comparatively mild temperature of the north-west of Europe is attributed mainly to the influence of the Gulf Stream, which carries from a tropica! region of the earth a great amount of heat, to he expended on otherwise cheerless shores. To the influence of the Gulf j tion respecting them is imp rfect. There is one Stream the moist climate of Great Britain, and especially of Ireland, is due and to the same oause is owing the rain whioh our north-oastern are pretty sure to bring. The introduction of a large body of heated water into a oolder region, it may readily bo imagined, produoes many atmosphere and electrical changes, and hence the title of þÿ weather þÿbreeder, which we are told Sailors bestow on the Gulf Stream. of Mexico is replaced by an equatorial current, whioh crosses tH ocean from the coast of Africa, and enters the Caribbean Sea Between the Gulf Stream on the north and this equatorial current on the south, lies a region which is known as the Sargassa Sea Aooording to Lieutenant Maury, it oover.-t an area equal in extent to the whole Mississippi valley, and is so thickly matted over with gulf weeds that the speed of vessels passing through it is often much retarded, and it sometimes appear to the eye solid enough to walk on. This phenomenon is attributed to the fact of the S irgassa Sea being the centre of a whirl of whioh the equatorial current forms one portion and the Gulf Stream another. Tho Atlantic Ocean has been compared to a basin of water, in which, when the fluid is set into rapid motion, there is a tendency in any light subttanoe that may be floating on the outside to whirl to the oentre of the basin, and the presence of this drift in a cdkparatively motionless sea is taken as one evidence of the existence of a circular ourrent in tho Atlantic, flowing westward to the great American gulf, rushing out through the Straits of Florida, aud sweeping with a wido curve to the shores of Northern Europe, from which a current sets to the south along tho coast of Europe and Africa. It is very common for bottles containing a slip of paper, with the name of the ship, and its precise latitude and longitude, to be thrown overboard in different parts of the world, and the plaees in whioh these bottles
are picked up after the lapse of a considerable time, indicate the general direction of the currents From experiments of this nature it ap-

A bottle dropped overboard at Cape Horn is picked up in the Caribbean Sea; another dropp d off the coast of Africa makes its appear- l mice in the Gull Stream off tue coast of Ireland, aud is there thrown on shore ; a third, escaping the shore, voyages along the coast of Europe to j the African seas again, thus completing the circle. There are other currents in the Atlantic, the most impoitunt of which are those setting towards the equator trom the Polar seas, and via versa. There is thus a constant interchange of water between the tropical, and arctio and antarctic regions of the globe, þÿ an exchange at- j tended with tin most beneficial results, Serving to amelioiate the cold of the one, and to modify the heat of the other. The cold stream which runs with great rapidity from þÿBaffin s Bay and the coast of Labrador, to the southwards, meets the Gulf stream off the Great Banks. It then divides into two portions, one of which passes under the Gulf Stieam, and finds its way not improbably to the Caribbean Sea, for the temperature of the water there, at a little depth, is much below that of the crust of the earth, and as cold as it is off t be shores of the Arctic Seas ; the other runs southward, a surface current, along the shores of the United Slates, between them and the Gulf Stream. LOSS OF A RUSSIAN VESSEL OF THE LINE. 826 LIVES LOST. Th e Journal of St. Pifrrshurg of the 1st
communicated by order of the Minister of þÿ It has pleased Providence I should par-

that can happen at sea, and to make me a witness of the instantaneous and inexplicable loss of one of the vessels in my fleet. A few minutes have sufficed for a beautiful ship of the line, thoroughly seaworthy, to be engulphed by the waves during a tempestuous night. Not a cry of distress reached us from the scene of the disaster, although we were but four þÿcables length distant windward. No one survives to explain to us the cause of this unparalleled catastrophe. On the 28th Aug. (Sept. 9) four ships of the line, the Imperatrice Alexandra, the Valdimir, the Lelort of 84 guns, and the Pamiat Asova, of 74 guns, which were in the port of Revel, received orders to arm and return to Cronstadt. Ten days afterwards the Pamiat Asova quitted the roads, towed by a steam-frigate. The three other vessels were ready to set sail two days later; they had water and provisions for a month, and their stowage was the same as at the end of their cruise in the preceding year ; the Lefort was thoroughly repaired at Cronstadt in 1862. I had received instructions to profit by the favourable weather to set sail, without waiting for the steam-tugs. On the 9th of September (21st), I got under sail with beautiful weather and a favourable breeze from S.S.W., the barometer marking 29.79 English. A little later the wind freshened, and abreast of the island of Rothskar we took in two reefs in the topsails. At halfpast 8 p.m., after passing the Island of Hochland, the fleet was making more than II knots. The wind increasing, I ordered

a third, and then a fourth reef, to be taken in. The barometer being at 29-16, and the weather foggy, we sailed as close as possible to the wind, endeavouring to keep our course by short tacks, until morning ; each time I gave the signal for the manoeuvre. At half-past 11 the wind shifted to the West, at midnight to the N W., and at 4 þÿo clock to the North, with squalls and snow. At daybreak we were near the island of Grand-Tuters. The fleet was on the starboard tack, the Imperatrice Alexandra a little to windward, and the Vladimir in the wake of the Lefort, with four reefs in her topsails. At a distance of five miles from Tuters we veered, during our manoeuvre the Lefort appeared to us as if wishing to veer ; suddenly a violent squall laid her on her side. Though her sails were let go, she leaned over so much to larboard that wc expected her masts would go, but she continued gradually to lean over till she foundered in the short time that the Vladimir took to tack about. The keel of the Lefort appeared once, and was then swallowed up in the waves. Exclusive of the Commander and 12 officers, the vessel had on board 743 seamen, 63 women and 17 children ; all perished. This disaster took place on September 10th (22nd), at 23 minutes past 7 a.m., at 6£ miles to the N.N.E. of the island of Grand-Tuters, at a depth of 30 fathoms. After this unparalleled catastrophe, the wind continuing to increase, we brailed up the fore-top sails and top-gallant sails, and afterwards

the main-top sails, and decided to anchor at a depth of 31 fathoms, letting out all the cable of two anchors. Fifty-three hours afterwards the wind calmed, and the steamers arriving in the meantime, towed us to Cronstadt. þÿ Signed by the Rear-Admiral þÿ Nobdman þÿI.

The Manufacture of Words. þÿ No permission has been so much abused in our days as that of Horace for the manufacture of words. He allows men to mould one now and then, with a modest discretion and caution ; but he is addressing poets, not vendors of patent leather or dealers in 1

$T«, Gs&QliS A V t %, marine stores. Would he not have stood aghast at the term þÿ an tig ropy þÿlos ? Would it not puzzle a Scaliger or Bentley ? It is time, we protest, to put a stop to these vile coinages when every breeches-maker or blacking manufacturer invents a compound word of six syllables as expressive ot his wares. Ladies do not wear petticoats now-a-days, but crinolines. What is their new name for garters? Men do not ride on horseback as aforetime þÿ they take equestrian exercise; women are not married like their grand-mothers þÿ they are led to the hymeneal altar. A bookseller, forsooth, becomes a bibliopole ; and a servant is converted into a manciple. Barbers do not sell toothpowder and shaving-soap as their fathers did, butodonto, and dentifrice, and rypophagoti ; hairwash has passed away þÿ it is capillary fluid. Can any one tell us what is the meaning of þÿ as applicable to disease? If it has a signification at all, we will guarantee to find halt a-dozen Saxon monosyllables expressive of the same idea. Medical Gentlemen, too, talk of phlebotomy ; we know that it has some connexion with bloodletting, and, for our own part, we always associate the term with a night we once spent between the sheets, all alive O ! in an Irish hotel. Who would believe that þÿ epistaxis means simply bleeding at the nose? Fancy one school-boy doubling his fist, and telling another to þÿ look out for þÿ epistaxis.'' What is meant by that fashionable word þÿ aesthetics? We take up the first book

within reach, and open it at random. It is n ill mm IVordsicorth ; a Biography, by Edwin Paxton Hood. Well, what do we þÿ read ? þÿ is simply intended a life in its ideal atti- By aesthetic þÿbiography, he says, suing. tudes, Simply intended ! Did ever mortal man listen to such verbiage run mad ? What, again, are we to understand by the words þÿ objective" and þÿ subjective," which every goose with his sham metaphysics has nowadays on his lips ? These Titanic Gilfillanisms will certainly be the death of us. þÿ b razor's Magazine for September.

Sir Janies Clark of England has assailed with considerable force the doctrine that a change of climate is beneficial to persons suffering with consumption ; and a French physician, M. Carriere, has written forcibly against it. Dr. Burgess, an eminent 8cotch physician, also contends that climate has little or nothing to do with the cure of consumption, and that, if it had, the curative effects would be produced through the skin and not the lungs. That a warm climate is not in itself beneficial, he shows from the fact that the disease exists in all latitudes. In India and Africa, tropical climates, it is as frequent as in Europe and North America. At Malta, right in the heart of the genial Mediterranean, the army reports of England show that one-third of the deaths among the soldiers are by consumption. At Nice, a favorite resort of English invalids, especially those afflicted with lung complaints, there are more native-born persons die of consumption than in any English town of equal population. In Geneva the disease is almost equally prevalent. In Florence, pneumonia is said to be marked by a suffocating character, and by a rapid progress toward its last stage. Naples, whose climate is the theme of so much praise by travellers, shows in her hospitals a mortality by consumption equal to one in two and one-third, whereas Paris, whose climate is so often pronounced villainous, the proportion is only one in three and one-quarter. In Madeira, no local disease is more common than con-
sumption.

POSTPONEMENT OF THE ATLANTIC TE LEGRAPH ENTERPRISE. The directors of the Atlantic Telegraph Company have resolved to postpone the laying of their cable until next year. This is prudent. It would be an ill-advised step to risk the attempt in October, when the natural obstacles of wind and weather might of themselves entail a second lailure. There are many new points in the conduct of the enterprise to be considered, and there is, doubtless, much room for improvement in the necessary machinery. It has been urged that (he breaks for regulating the paying out of the cable should not be left to the judgment and attention of any man, no matter how great his skill, but should be governed by a self-acting apparatus. This is obviously a wise and practical suggestion. There are others, too, which merit attention. To prevent the recurrence of such a disaster as that which has already taken place, it is thought advisable to pass the cable through a series of buoys, or, better still, through a second vessel employed for the purpose, so that in case of a break, the wire may be recovered ere it disappears into deep water. These and other suggestions that have been offered are worthy of that earnest consideration which, vve doubt not, will he given to them. When the effort to lay the cable shall be renewed next summer, we hope to see every possible accident provided against, and the greatest enterprise of the age finally crowned with success þÿ þÿHarper Weekly s Journal.

From the. St. Thomas Times, October 31.) SAVfO B.MHGO (From La Gaceta, published at Santiago.) .Translated for the þÿ Tidende. When Mars and Bellona take an active part in political questions, resorting to the eloquence of artillery, and directing arguments with the of the i%ord, it would appear that the powerful and as Guteuiberg action, element by courtesy leave the field free of should restrain mon. 40 1 to the new combatants. But, it does not so occur, after the explosion of a bomb-shell, and previous to the complicated discussion of bayonets, press in its turn opens its batteries and þÿ powerful the detonation of cannon, and the effects of the press

succession of shells directed against the main body of an army. For this reason we now see, that in ali countries where questions which could not be solved by their Cabinets, and are consigned to the field ot battle, the press agitates, and interferes itself, and perhaps while the drums and trumpets are inciting the wrath of the soldier, publio opinion is surprised by the appearance of an idea which, as a Diviue spark discovers reason, and attracts things toward an understanding which avoids all the catastrophe attendant on strife in which humanity is always the victim- In accordance with such principles let us asceud the tribuuc, and from the cool and delicious hank of the Yakey we will discuss with concern the same question which the regenerating army is new discussing at the mouth of the Ozama. Lot us therefore consider Baez locked up within the walls of St. Domingo resisting the will of the nation, and behind the FikE which, in that stage, the defenders of Liberty are exchanging with the þÿrebels let us raise our voice to explain to those few citizens who have escaped from the great majority what are the causes which have brought the Republic on the field of Insurrection. We will thus accomplish a duty and render a service to our country. The advent of Baez to power, was not the work of patriotism þÿ the Republic is aware of itþÿ it lias the conscience, although we blush to avow it, that the Presidency of Baez was thrust upon it

þÿ by force of circumstances, the memory whereof wounds the national honor, and iu addition, it ! might be said, that society accepted him rather as a tribute to the tranquillity of the country, than in the idea that iu his administration any advantage would accrue to the Dominican people. Baez himself well understood his position þÿ his first acts 'revealed his want of confidence, and through this he lound himself constrained to offer with euergetio protestations of security, the realization of a splendid programme which, later, he would have to rend in fragments and to deny and contradict in the most cynical mauner. He told the nation on assuming power that he bore no anger ; that before the Altars of the country he hud abandoned all resentment, and that the highest ambition at which he aimed was to uuito and render his fellow-citizens þÿhappy ; he also said that tLere should be no gallows, no proscriptions, no arbitrary þÿimprisonment that the public fund should be administered with probity, and ultimately that he would strive to insure the national independence by obtaining an honorable arrangement with the Haytian Empire, and maintaining free and true friendly relations with nations abroad. In this manner Baez was installed in power. Without any prestige in the army, as those brave defenders of the country had never seen him at their side in any of the actions which are registered in our achievement, without the slightest inclination of public opinion in his favor, as is proved by the result of the

electoral college in this Province, where alone independence was found in the unhappy votes which gave to the Republic a President so thrust. Baez consequently presented hitnself to the nation, with falsehood on his lips, to endeavour to form a circle in order to support him, and there is no doubt but that he succeeded in attracting to the side of a small party of corrupt þÿmen a part of the most imprudent youths of St. Domingo. The.citizens of this place will remember with horror the scandalous outrages which were committed against the publio order in the first days of that strange administration. Groups of dangerously armed persons, running through the streets, and threatening with death, the families of the most respectable, returning to disband themselves at the Government House where Baez prepared for them the most lowed orgies This was one of the means with which the new authority sought to form a party for itself. He knew quite well that the citizens of good seuse had rejected him, and that it was impossible to put his treacherous plans into execution without having the aid of a number of compromised individuals who would make common cause with him in case of danger. Indeed, Baez did not commence operations until after he had launched out those who now so obstinately accompany him, beginning by violating the solemn convention which, through the diplomatic Body, he had entered into from St. Thomas with the General Libertador.

This felonious act was followed up by the imprisonment of General Francisco Sosa and other distinguished military men, and the abuse and persecution of respectable citizens, showing especially his chief prejudice against the persons of note in these Provinces. It would require too much time and space to present, if possible, a sketch of all the arbitrary acts with which Baez initiated his ephemeral administration. It would suffice, alone, for the Republic to determine on its complaints upon the disorders which have been committed in the Treasury department to justify the revolution into which the country has had to throw itself. The monstrous issue of paper-money does it not fully prove that þÿBaez s ideas were no other than to turn to his own advantage the fortunes of the nation ? What man, however inexperienced he may be in economical affairs, can do otherwise than he astounded to see a Government instead of favoring the public credit, sink it, into the most terrible confusion ? Baez has sacrificed the Republic, and in that sacrifice lias committed the infamy to drag in as accomplices a circle of young men of whom the couutry had much to hope Let the anathemas, the odium and the execration of the Dominican people fall on Baez ! CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 17TH NOVEMBER. 1857. The public, will no doubt, be surprised to learn that the manager of the Estate Enfield Green, Mr. KoEFof.d, has been acquitted by the Centre District's Police Court of the charge of having bribed the. labourer MahoNV to enter in his service. Flushed by bis success Mr. KoEford has instituted a suit against this Journal for defamntid n of character ! ! The right which we have exercised is that of a public journalist to give the particulars, as known at the time, of a caso which intimately concerns the public, as affecting the best inter-

eats of the Island ; and if Mr. Koefok.d has succeeded in proving the act charged on him to be no act of bribery but a simple "'loan, " we congratulate him on his success. We feel, however, convinced that if our condemnation or acquittal in this suit, depended on a verdict of a jury, composed of members of this community, we should have very little fear of the result ; and, even as it is, his success in this suit shall not cause us to relinquish the right ot expressing public opinion on any similar occasion.

» From the St. Thomas Times, November 1 1 SAM TO DOMINGO Our' columns to-day will be lbund to contain a decree from the President of the Dominican Republic, placing under blockade all the Ports of Santo Domingo, excepting that. of the Capital, which is no doubt convenient. This prodigious step, we are told, is resorted to only at the last moment when blind obstinacy seem still to pursue the rebels. We are further told that in order to make the decree respected a sufficient number of vessels will invest the coast ! i. e. a lew dug-out buncos ! Alas ! tor the power of human comprehension, and to realize these startling truths, we must remove ourselves to continental shades, and there contemplate those "glorious paper blockades" that were once wont to startle Europe and strike terror into hearts of British Oak, but who with ail scoured the Mediterranean, German Ocean, Bay of Biscay, &c., &c., ami successfully held blocked up within their own waters to have put into effect that which " paper" those phantom ships that were practically represented. But seriously, the President, who, from all that is told, we must suppose is himself under blockade, to while away the hours of monotonous time, and to escape the miscries of unwelcome contemplation, must have again turned student, ami in unfolding the pager, of history must have stumbled over one of those farces which formed the interlude in those days of sanguinary tragic Europe. and it has bethought him that to re-enact those scenes on the stages of Santo Domingo would be to give a greater farci-

cal colouring to the general pantomime that is already being played there. It is our very firm conviction that few if any nations will be found disposed to respect the blockade of Mr. President Bakz, from the very well-known fact that he does not possess an adequate force to make it respected, a requisite which weighs heavily in the conclusions of maritime powers in modern times in how far blockades are henceforth to receive the sanction of international law when thus fiiinsily instituted. We need hardly say, that to the navigator with the least daring, and an adventurous turn of mind. Mr. lt.u'z will find his blockade proving of little or no avail, as such adventurous spirits will sail in arid out of the ports of Santo Domingo with little regard tor his crvizcrs.

From " The West Indian Harbados, Nov. 5. DEMERARA. The intelligence which has reached this City from the gold mines at Upata, is encouraging to gold seekers. About 2,000 ounces found their way to Bolivar during the mon tli of September, but there must have becti very much more retained in the hands of the gold diggers, and large quantities have been smuggled out of tlie country to evade the duty of 10 per cent, levied upon gold by the government of Venezuela. That the mines are very productive there cannot be the slightest doubt. We have authentic accounts lying before us, in which

t þÿ & R, 0 I X, A Y i it is stated, that one party of gold seekers found, from the 1st to the 20th of August, 32 ounces of gold ; a second party in six weeks procured 80 ounces of gold ; a third party, who has been working since January last, had collected 174 lbs. (avoirdupois) of gold ; a fourth party found a nugget weighing 46 ounces; anil a fifth party found a piece of pure gold five inches long by two and a half thick, its shape was that of a bar slightly curved, and it weighed 24 ounces. From the correspondence which has taken place between her Majesty's Vice-Consul at Bolivar and the Governor of the Province, it appears, that the Government of Venezuela view with feelings of indefinite apprehension ihe visit of the Commissioners, who are gone to explore the interior of this Colony towards the eastern frontier, and to visit, in the course of their travels the gold mines on the Yuruari. Instructions have been issued to the Magistrates in the Canton ot Upata to arrest the progress of these gentlemen, and to convey tliein to Bolivar to obtain the perinisston of the Venezuelan Government before they proceed to Fulfil the objects of their mission, so far as the exploration of the gold districts are concerned. We are not disposed to attach too much importance to the proceedings of the Governor of the Province of Guyana, who, in the exuberance of his zeal and patriotism, lias determined to be uncourteous towards the gentlemen who have gone from this colony on a visit to the gold fields of the Yurnari. He appears

to entertain a grave apprehension that we arc desirous of seizing the gold producing district and claiming it as a part of the British territory, the boundaries of which have never been defined. lie has got hold of an idea, that a railway is about to be constructed from Demerara to the Diggings at Tupuquen; and he seriously believes it. Where he got this intelligence from we cannot imagine ; but no such impracticable scheme has ever been mooted in this colony; and if the Governor of Venezuelan Guyana, had been aware of the geographical and physical features of the country, lie would have known that the construction of a railway through sucli a country, would be the last thing that any sane man would contemplate or attempt. We do not apprehend that the Commissioners from the Colony will be put to any further inconvenience, than the loss of time and delay which will be occasioned by their being taken out of the course they had marked out for themselves. There is, however, some ground for hoping that they may not be placed under the disagreeable necessity of going to Bolivar, for the purpose of asking permission to continue their explorations, as the Governor and his private Secretary have gone to Tupnquen with Mr. Bratt, a mineralogist, who has been sent by the government from this colony, to inspect the gold fields, and (we presume) to make himself familiar with the geological features of the country, prior to an exploring expedition being despatched to pros-

pect in the interior of this colony. The Governor may there meet with the Commissioners, and probably hall an hour's conversation may settle the whole difficulty. That gold will be discovered here eventually, there is not the slightest doubt. | Specimens of quartz containing gold have been brought into the city lrom the intn- | rior ; and a few days ago, a piece of quartz containing traces of gold was found on the i macadamized streets of the City. This i stone had been brought from the neighbourhood of the Penal Settlement ; and it | has been known for years that gold is to I be found in that locality. The effort that was being made by the ! Merchants and others in this City to despatch a private expedition into the interior

with the view of prospecting for gold, js likely to prove abortive þÿ not for the lack of money, but for the lack of men. We hear of some arrangements having been made to send off a party for that purpose ; but we have no more confidence in the result of such an expedition, than we have in the result of the celebrated Shanks' expedition to the Cuyuni Both will cost large sums of money, but neither will find the gold. At least, if they do, they will stumble across it by accident. There is a fine field open here for an active enterprising geologist. Such a man would be a real acquisition in this Colony ; and he would be certain to realize a fortune, as from the geological features of the country, the mineral treasures of the interior must be rich beyond conception. þÿ Colonist, Oct. 23.

(From the "New York Times," Oct. 23 | Danish Consul-General. We understand that M. de Raasloff has been appointed charge d'affaires and Consul-General lor Denmark in the United States. lie has resided in this country for several years past, and lias become widely known as a gentleman of high character and marked ability. Originally connected with the Danish army, he became known by sundry important improvements in the firearms used, and also, at a subsequent date, by a book recording the result of observations made in Algeria during a service of seven years in the French army. He wrote a series of very able papers upon the Sound Dues question some months since, which were published first bi the columns of the Times, and afterwards in a pamphlet, and which discussed that subject much more ably than any other publication upon it. Mr. Raasloff has the grant from his Government of the right to construct a submarine Telegraph to connect the several islands of her West India possessions, and is now engaged in the prosecution of that work. He is expected to arrive here during the month of November.

COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir ! I visited the examination of the Danish School in this town to-day, and heard as much as circumstances permitted me to hear. The examination was conducted as usual ; and left me to find the same fault as I did on a former occasion viz : that the higher classes, both boys and girls, ought to be examined, consonant with their acquirements, in the same room ; in order that the visitors might have the pleasure of hearing both. The going from one room to the other is perfectly tiresome, and, as

I conceive, has this effect on visitors as well as þÿchildren, a wondering what is going on in the next room ; and ai. a ixicty to witness it. '! o icin.dy this would, I feel convinced, give to the next examination moie the appearance of things being done as they ought to be done. Of the examination, as it was conducted, I shall only remark, that it could at once be seen that the method by the present teachers 'n the instructing of the children, is hut in its infaucy ; and that time alone is requi cd to test its efficacy. There is no doubt, therefore, that after the present teachers will have been there for some longer time þÿ say before the next examination that þÿ there will he a grand improvement in the Upper School. A. TEA HER. Frederiksted, November IStli 1867.

(From the New York 'tribune.) ABOLITION IN THE DUTCH WEST INDIES. The abolition of Slavery in the Dutch West Indies, about to be proposed in thq, States-General of Holland, is of less importance from the numbers upon whom it may confer the boon of Liberty than from i he new prool it affords of the growing force of the sentiment of humanity among all civilized nations. Upon the continent of South America the Dutch once held very extensive possessions. The Dutch West India < ompany carried on fora time a successful struggle with Portugal for the possession of the Brazil. But the insurrection of the conquered Portuguese before long expelled tlieui from those regions, leav ing them in South America, only their settlements on the River Belize, Demerara and Essequibo. Even these districts, however, arc no longer Dutch. they passed During the wars the into ot the French Revolution, hands ot the English, and now constitute the colony cf British Guiana. All that remains to the Dutch of South American territory, constituting in fact, their principal possession in America, is the colony of Surinam, between British Guiana on the west and French Guiana or t 'ayenrie, on th#i ast þÿ a colony the more interesting to us from the circumstance that, having once been English, it was yielded up to the Dutch at the peace of Breda, in 1667, in exchange for the piovince ot New Netherlands and the. city of New Amsterdam, ot which the English laid taken forcible possession three years before, changing the name of both to New York.
There was considerable discussion among the noliticiaus and nolitical economists of

the times, whether in makig this exchange England had not made a very bad bargain. In point ot extent of territory, both colonic., stood about on a level; Neither had any detiuile boundaries inland, and both claimed a large extent of unsettled territory. As their respective boundaries have since been established, Surinam, so far as square miles are concerned, has taken the lead. The exteut of that colony is reckoned by geographers at about sixty thousand square miles, while we of New-York, after claiming during the progress of the Revolutionary War, all Upper Canada, and all the country between the lakes, the Ohio, and the Mississippi, have been cut down to forty-six thousand square miles. At the time of the exchange, now near two centuries ago, the population of the colonies were pretty nearly equal ; and indeed for the next hundred years Surinam kept pretty equal progress with New-York, and at times, especially after the introduction of the cultivation of coffee, first carried there from Java about 17fS, and under the impulse of the slave trade, it seemed to justify the arguments of those who had maintained that a colony in the tropics, of such extent and fertility, Was of far greater value than New-York could ever be. The first blow to the prosperity of Surinam grew out of an insurrection of the negroes, a body of whom escaped into the uninhabited district in the rear of the colony, where they maintained themselves agaiust every attempt at their subjugaton. Finally, the colonists could

do no better than to enter into a treaty of peace with them. Another insurrection of the same sort broke out about the time of our revolutionary war; and Captain Stedman, who served as one of a party of English mercenaries enlisted to tight the rebel negroes, lias given in his book on Surinam a very interesting description of the colony as he saw it. This war ended, like the former, in a recognition of the revolted negroes as free and independent, they, however, entered into a stipulation not to harbor runaways from the plantations. There is no very recent account of Surinam, but these two independent negro communities still exist, we believe, in the interior. During the wars of the French Revolution Suiiuam, like the restofthe Dutch colonies was ccupied by the English; but although they kept the adjoining territory now const tuting British Guiana, at the peace of IS I Surinam was restored to the Dutch. During the English. occupation a large part of the plantations had passed into the hands of English propietors, and it is chiefly, we believe, to English proprietors that they still belong. Ever since the abolition of the slave trade the population of Surinam has been on the decline. An official return, dated in 1S42, gave for the total population, 56,000. Ot these, 2.50J were whites, ot whom half were Christiana aud half Jews The coloured population (population of mixed blood) was reekeiid at 7,000, of whom 4,0.0 were free aud 3C0J slaves. The black population was set down at þÿ46.5 0, of-

whom only 1,500 were free. Paramaribo, the capital, had a population of 15,000, including' 2,000 whites The decrease in the population of the colony in the preoeeding ten years was reckoned at 8,000, caused by the aunual diminution of slaves. According to a statement purporting to be official, contained in the Surinam. C our ant , the number of slaves in Surinam on the 1st of January, lfcfiU, was as follows : belonging to plantations, males, 14,190 þÿ females, 14,942 ; belonging to persons not planters, males, 4 032 þÿ females, 4,934 ; total, 33,098 ; showing in the last fourteen years a diminution of 10,000. It is evident j-rom these figures that the alternative is betweeu

St. Eustatius, at the liuie ot our Revolutionary War, was, a a neutral islaud, a seat of trade, similar to that which St. Thomas afterwrd became ; but it never-recovered from the blow which it received iu being plundered aud sold out at a military auction by Admiral Rodney, and, with its neighbors of isuba and St. Martin's, it has uo\v but a few hundred inhabitants, wtiose chief employment is the cultivation of tropica! fruits for exportation to this city. Bou Air, Amba and Ouragoa have a vory dry climate, aird are chiefly known for their saltpans, specially the former The thousand or two slaves on this island employed in the salt works appear to be a cross between tbe Indian aud þÿnegro a good-looking, sprightly race, who speak a sort of broken Portuguese. Curvyoa, which ouce had the same Governor with ourselves iu the person of Petrus Stuyvesaut, has a few plautatious, and perhaps two or three thousaud slaves. Harney's Staff, arrived at this post yesterday morning, on his way to the States from Great Salt Lake City. lie was detached by the General, at the beginning oi August, to proceed to Utah, to gather necessary information concerning- the disposition of the inhabitants, the geography of the routes to the Territory, the condition ot the crops, &c., and to report to headquarters. He returns with news which, perhaps, justifies inferences that the Utah complication will present in history toe most prominent feature ot tile administration of Mr. Buchanan. Tiie expression of a determination to resist the entrance of the newlyappointed officials, aud of the U. S. army

into Utah, is unanimous among the people of the Territory. You are probably aware already of the result of his mission, for a courier, bearing dispatches to the headquarters of the army, preceded his arrival here one day, reaching this post on the evening of Saturday the 20th, and departing the same night. But, in view of its important character, the following details cannot fail to be interesting. Capt. Van Vliot arrived at Salt Lake City Sept. on 8 and remained there a week His measurement of its distance from this post, by the Odometer, was 518 miles, corresponding very nearly with that of Capt Stansbury in 1849. Adding to it the ais tance of Fort Laramie from Fort Leavenworth, 628 miles, as measured by Brevet Col. Smith, who arrived here on Saturday in command of Companies A and D of the Tenth Infantry, who were detained in Minnesota from their regiment, the total distance of the city from Fort Leavenworth is 1,146 miles, 22 miles less than that given by Capt. Stansbury. He left his escort on Ham's Fork, about twenty miles west of Green River, and proceeded to the city, attended only by his own servants. He had been assured by every party he encountered en route for the States that his visit would be attended with personal danger ; but, on the contrary, he was received and treated with the utmost hospitality, offered many facilities for ascertaining the condition of the Territory and the disposition of the inhabitants, and no obstacle was put to his departure.

An official dinner was given in his honor by Heber C. Kimball, and lie had daily interviews with Brigham Young and the other dignitaries of the Mormon Church. Their expressed determination, from first to last, was this : to resist at all hazards the ingress of the troops this Autumn. When they were reminded of the certainty that in case their resistance one year should be effectual, a force would be dispatched to Utah the next, against which twice their population in arms would strive in vain to close the passes, they rpplied that they had considered all that, and that when such a force had stormed those passes, they would enter a valley in which not one shrub would be green nor one stone remain upon another. They took pains to show him their gardens and vineyards, their harvest, barns, houses, and live stock, and to contrast their present prosperity with such a scene of desolation. Their object now, they said, was to gain time to enable the National Government to retrace its steps, and they intend to present their case to Congress through their delegate, Dv. They said that thev would regard the entrance of the troops as the beginning of a repetition of their sufferings at Kirtland, Independence and Nunvoo; that they had learned a lesson from experience, and would now meet aggression at the start, and

resist the wedge before it should enter the wood ; if they could not keep the troops out this year they would sacrifice all for their religion, take to the mountains, and fight a war of glory and extermination. EUROPEAN INTELLIGENCE In an article on the late even's in India the Constitutionnel pays the following tribute to the noble qualities there displayed by our unfortunate countrymen "If anything could soften the bitterne-s inspired by the sad news from India, it is assuredly the spectacle presented by the gallaut men who have fallen victims to this rebellion. %he dignity of the British character and the admirable strength of the Anglo Saxon race, which has performed so great a part in the history of the world, shine forth with splendour. Among the officers of the revolted regiments there were many young men who, by their youth and iuexperience, may s have contributed to the events which have swept them away ; but they have wiped out all faults by the firmness, free from any ostentation, they exhibited in late eveuts. vVe have described more than one deed of heroism worthy the admiration of posterity. In the midst of torments and on the brink of the grave they have displayed that modest courage which characterizes in our days the man ennobled by the influence of Christian civilization. The cruelty of the murderers has only been equalled by the courage of the victims. A nation which loses such sons must doubtless bewail their martyrdom, but it lias the right to be proud of them." The Nouvelliste of Marseilles publishes a letter which gives 6ome details of the murder of the Chancellor of the Neapolitan Consulate at Alexandria, already briefly mentioned by telegraph : þÿ 44 On the evening of the 9th of August M.

Gaetan Citati, a French subject, and Chancellor ot the Consulate of Naples was assassinated in the public square at Alexandria. M. Citati had long resided at Algiers as a merchant, and bad only been in Alexandria about two months as Chancellor of the Neapolitan Consulate, and has fallen through an act of vengeance, not directed against the man so much as against the situation which he filled There have been during the last year several assassinations at Alexandria among Italians, and the inquiry into th"se criminal affairs has been carried on by the Neapolitan Chancellor. The guilty persons were on the point of being discovered, when the Clnr e; received some anonymous threats w'.iah i u 1 him to resign his situation. M Citati replaced him, and in his turn received similar menaces, but he paid no attention to tbern, and performed his duty. The assassin has not been discovered. The consuls have had a meeting in order to adopt some effectual measure to put an end to such scenes, and they have determined that for the future the local police shall have access to European houses, which has been hitherto prohibited. Numerous arrests have taken place, and it is said that the police have laid their hands on an organized band of these desperadoes, almost exclusively composed of Italiaus." The following is a translation of a letter of July 4 received by the Augsburg Gazette from Calcutta :þÿ " Since the departure of the lai-t mail our position has got worse rather than better It is

now placed beyond all doubt that we have not only to do with a revolution in the native army, but also with a revolution of the whole of the Mahomedan population of India. The plan is to murder all Europeans and Christians, aud to restore the ancient Mahomedan Empire. All the plans were well laid, and the object must have been attained if it had not been for the precipitancy of the 21st Native Regiment. The revolution was to have begun iti Calcutta, and not in Delhi. The 2d Regiment of Grenadiers was to have taken possession of the fort in Calcutta, and at the same time the 34ih Native Regiment was to have murdered all the Europeans residing at Barrackpore, and afterwards made the best of its way to Calcutta. The native artillery at Dumdum was to have acted in the same way, and to have assisted the 2d Regiment of Grenadiers in sinking the, ships in the Hooghly by means of the guns of the fort. The ships were to be sunk in order that no Europ ana might be able to escape. The body guard of the Governor-General (veterans taken from the differennt cavalry regiments) was to have murdered all the persons in the service of Government. The Mahomedans in the bazaar were to have, destroyed the railroad and teleaph. The

19th Regiment, after all the Europeans had been put to death, was to march towards the north, murdering aud plundering as it went. As has been said, the precipitancy of the 21st Regiment eaused the failure of the whole scheme. Six men belonging to the 21 Regiment of Grenadiers were arrested, but, instead of being hanged, they were bauishel for 40 years ; that is, they were allowed to go their way in peace As the plot had been discovered at Calcutta, the North-West Provinoes began to act, and the movement soon extended from Delhi and Meerut through the whole of India (Presidency of Bengal). Delhi is still in the hands of the rebels, and the loss of Contingent and the much-eulogized the European regiments is great. The Gwalior Ghoorkas fired on the besieging troops, and made common cause with the insurgents. When it was known that the Chinese expedition had reached Singapore and had sailed for Calcutta, the insurgents, who are spread all over the country, made an attempt to get possession of the fort in Diamond Harbour, but failed. " Government is alone to blame for what has happened. Lord Dalhousie laid the foundation ot the thing, and Lord Canning thought himself so wise that he scorned to listen to either counsel or warning. The following statement will show what the Indian Administration is, how secure the Government felt, and how well planned the revolution was. In November last old Gholab Singh, who was well known to the publio during the Sikh war, wrote to Lord Canning that the

Mahomedans intended to rise and overthrow the British Government, and had offered hitn the direction of the projected movement. The Government laughed, arid did not even reply to the letter. Mr. Hamilton, a merchant in Cawnporo and Allahabad, who had gained the confidence of the native dealers, received notice to send away his family within six months At first he refused to do so, but at last he followed the well-meant oounsel. At the same time he wrote to the Government and offered to obtain further information, but received no reply to his letter. (A copy of the letter is in the hands of the booksellers Tkucker, Spick, and Co ) If I should inform you in my next letter that the Government has been driven away ( verjagt ), yen must not be astonished. This evening there is to be an 'Independence dinner' in the Townhall, and afterwards a meeting is to be held there. The meeting intends to draw up a petition to the Queen of England, praying her to take the reins of government into her owu hands, and to appoint a provisional administration for the moment. I could mention the name of the proposed President of the Provisional Government, but do not think it advisable to do so at present."

I have learnt that several alterations of considerable interest to the public have been made in the terms of the concession granted to M. de Normann for laying down a submarine telegraph from Sicily to Malta, and from Sicily to Cape Bon, by the Island of Pantellaria. According to these alterations each line is to be independent. If, after 15 or 20 years, it be found that the line does not pay the concession is to be annulled at the will of the concessionnaire. Despatches through may be sent in English, French, or Italian, instead of, as at present, only in French or Italian. Lastly, the Government, for secret service, will lay down a separate wire through the kingdom and a separate submarine wire through the Straits at their own expense. These new conditions are all of great importance, and those who have had any experience in continental telegraphs will well know how to appreciate the permission to send despatches in English. The line of transmission (to omit smaller interve. ing places) will be from Malta to Alga Grande, Regio, Messina, Naples, Rome, Bologna, Moena, Trieste, through Prussia, Holland, the Hague, and so on to the office in Lothbury. From all that I can hear the undertaking is being urged on with considerable activity, a guarantee for which would be the fact that the Electric and International Telegraph Company have taken the matter up, as I have already mentioned. This Government, too, appears to be in earnest, His Majesty having given personal orders

to ft high officer of his Court to proceed to Sicily and superintend the laying down of the wires across the island to Alga Grande. Similar despatch will be exercised as regards the submarine from Reggio to Messina, which might have been laid down long ago had it not been for obstacles offered by the season and by the Government, which pretended to a guarantee from M. de Normann to keep the submarine secure for a year. I believe the concessionnaire, or, perhaps, the Electric and International, have been in correspondence with the British Government, the India-house, and the Oriental and Peninsular Company on the subject of the newly-projected line, and the best hopes are entertained that their countenance and assistance will be secured.

The Bat of þÿVulcano. During the Greek war of independence, it was a frequent custom to send the vessels whose sheathing had become incrusted with shells, pebbles, and earthy matter, as is generally the case after a long voyage, to the Bay of Vulcano, in the Island of Santorin (26 leagues North of Candia). After a stay of only a few hours in that bay, the incrustation above alluded to could be swept away from the copper sheathing with a common broom. This property of the waters of Vulcano was known throughout the East, but had seldom been turned to advantage, and had been quite neglected during the last few years. In 1866, however, the Greek Government resolved to put it to the test, and applied to Rear-Admiral Bouet Villaumez to send a vessel there by way of experiment. Accordingly, the Solon, an iron built ship, protected by a strong coating of red lead paint, and having her keel encumbered with a quantity of sea-weed and shells which adhere firmly to the surface, received orders to repair to the Bay of Vulcano, and to stay there three or four hours. This short stay, however, appeared to have no effect on the tenacity of the

8 tr e i a ij , v i; a , weeds, and the Solon proceeded to Canea and Milo with the usual incrustation on her keel. Nevertheless, on arriving at the latter place, the captain thought it best to try again, and to have the keel slightly brushed with a broom. This time the experiment was perfectly successful, and the Solon acquired an increase of speed of a mile per hour by the operation. Since then the experiment has been often repeated both by French and English vessels ; and it is now an acknowledged fact that fhe waters of the Bay of Vulcano have the singular property of cleansing the keels of ships. These waters have a fetid smell, and in calm weather jets of a reddish kind of water are seen issuing from the bottom, as if caused by some secret volcanic agency. Hence it may be presumed that a strong current of sulphuretted hydrogen gas is generated, which combines with the oxide ot copper of the sheathing, transforming it into a sulphuret ; and as it is the oxide which cements the shells and wires together, its transformation destroys their cohesion. Similar effects have been observed in the old port of Marseilles, where ( the sulphuretted hydrogen gas, instead of being produced by volcanic agency, is furnished by the sewers of the city.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, I 3TH OCTOBER. 1857. A case of some interest, we is now pending at the Police Court of the f entre District, the facts of the case being

5 T? , & ft 0 (j X, & Y I, a substantiation of the truth of "Custodia's" remarks published in our paper of the 29th September. A manager of an estate in Prince's quarter employs a labourer, named Martin, to entice a family in Northside Quarter as labourers on his estate. Martin, it appears, did not succeed and refused to make a second attempt. The ploughman was then sent and he succeeded in enticing the father of the family to take service on the estate tor a bribe of $40. After this arrangement had been entered into and the money paid the father of the family refused to leave the Estate in Northside Quarter ; but, it is said, retained the bribe. The particulars of the ease we would be very happy to publish if we could obtain them.

Prom t hi London Times, Hr.pt. 15.) TURKEY. Constantinople, Sept. 5. Every one at all familiar with the weak and vacillating mind of the Sultan was not a little astonished at the decision displayed by His Majesty during the late political crisis. Not ali the threats, nor aggressive acts of the confederate diplomatists, could make him yield; but, the struggle over and the battle won, his energy lias failed. Instead of following up his triumph, and shaking off all foreign influence, he has in one moment surrendered all the advantage gained, and by lending himself to a shameful intrigue proved once more to the world that he knows not how to be independent. He has consented to remove Iledschid Pasha from office. No one could blame the Sultan for this measure, did it appear that Redschid had in any way forfeited his master's confidence and goodwill ; but the Sultan himself bus taken care to let us know that such is not the case, by assuring Redschid, since his removal, that his confidence in him is still boundless, and his desire to avail himself of his services as great as ever, but that circumstances prevent him doing so for a while. What these circumstances are is soon told. Redschid has many enemies. During the late conflict, unmindful of their country's honour, they were leagued with the stranger. This policy failed, but Redschid ceased to be Grand Vizier, and some of their number into the Ministry. an important office, his influence was great, and it seemed likely that he would be soon again at the head of affairs. But it was represented to the Sul-

tan that it would be very agreeable to the French Ambassador and to the Emperor if the Minister who had so successfully resisted their demands were altogether sot aside. As diplomatic relations were resumed and M. de Thouvcnel would shortly have an official audience, such a measure would efface any remnant of bitterness lurking in the bosom ot that diplomatist, and be very grateful to the leelings of the Emperor. And so the only man who has shown any governing talent has ceased to belong to the Ministry ! He has been replaced by Fuad Pasha, who, it will be remembered, when last in office, made such a mess of the Bolgrad question that its solution seemed quite hopeless. A further change will probably soon take place. Mehemet, Kibrisli will become Grand Vizier, and then the party in power will have rallied all the talent it can command and try to hold its ground as long as it can. And this is how the game of Ministers is played here. Now one influence, now understand, another, disposes of the places ; as for the interests of the country or the opinions of the public, they are counted as nothing.

But the day is not far off when, evven in Turkey, the public voice will speak so loudly that it will force a hearing. Since the war the middle and even the lower classes of Turlt3 have singularly opened their eyes. They are beginning to see and feel that they are forgotten in the race of a few greedy Pashas alter the public money. They will not long consent to see the wealth and resources of their country squandered by improvident and incapable Ministers. The extravagant expenditure of the Sultan and his women, and the endless palaces he is every day building, are becoming common themes of discussion in all the cafuneks. Only two days ago, in the sacred suburb of Eyoub, the City of the Tombs, the abode of the most fanatic Mussulmans, the last place in Stamboul where one would expect to hear seditious language, a white-turbaned Turk, in the middle of a large group, asked me whether it was true that the Kings of England had wards of 200 years. " Why," said he, not built themselves a new palace for up- "our Padishahs build themselves one even year. How can a country be rich when its wealth is so heedlessly squandered f You are wise, and do not let your Kings do as they like." With all the religioue prestige which surrounds the Imperial person, such opinions need not gain much ground among the people to become serious. Hitherto, all attempts at reform in Turkey have been frustrated by the corruption of the upper classes. These constitute an army of placemen, dependent on

the State for their support- Accustomed to indulge themselves iti every luxury, they are obliged to invent perquisites, that they may afford themselves an expenditure far above their salaries. Nothing is to be expected from a class thus situated. Though they may possess talents, and acquire knowledge, they cannot acquire honesty ; their talents and knowledge they must apply to dishonest purposes. Unfortunately, this class is every day increasing ; Beys from the provinces, servants and slaves "of high functionaries, are every day receiving civil rank, and increasing the number of useless pensioners of the Government ; several thousand persons have been added to the list in less than a year. If there is any hope for Turkey it must rest on the middle and lower classes; here alone is still found the antique and proverbial honesty of the Turk. They are gradually developing themselves, learning the history of the world, and every day In coming more and more initiated into the real condition of their country. Th<y will rouse themselves to energy at no very remote period, and then woe to those who now so superbly lord it over them.

This is a serious matter in that little establishment ; 1 do not mean the cash, but the mistake in arithmetic ; for it occasions a world of Department, if the reports be true that so scrutiny. An error in balancing has been keep a delegation of from each office at work sometimes through the whole night. A hue and cry was of course made after this 100/., as i the old lady in Thread-needle-street would be in the Gazette for want of it. Luckily on the Sunday morning a clerk (in the middle of the sermon, I dare say, if the truth were known) felt a suspicion of the truth dart through his mind quicker than any flash of the telegraph itself. He told the chief casher on Monday morning that perhaps the mistake might have occurred in packing some boxes of specie for the West Indies, which had been sent to Southampton for shipment. (From tie London Times, Sept, 17.) De gustibus non est disputandum : this, we suppose, applies to all tastes, religious as well us other, the sublime and the mysterious, as well as the epicurean class of tastes. We must not dispute about enthusiasms. Everybody must be allowed to have his own enthusiasm. Here are many excellent people very enthusiastic about the " Evangelical Alliance ; there is a meeting at Berlin ; " long and heavily laden" trains full of enthusiastic gentlemen arrive, English, Americans, French, Germans, Protestant ministers of all denominations þÿ Church of England, Lutheran, Independent, Reformed Calvinist, Wesleyan Methodist. The most ample accommodation is provided for these visitors. Our stern Puritan forefathers met in wild and savage scenes, under the overhanging brows of mountain ridges and by the side of remote tarns and cataracts ; they preached to each other in the face of stormy skies; the arch of Heaven was their roof overhead, and the heather was their bed. Their descendants meet under happier auspices at Berlin ; " the office opened in the bureaux " information as to Deputies " of the House of hotel or lodging accom- supplies every " modation," and by a judicious combination the very ticket of admission to the religious conferences contains much useful information of this kind. This ingenious, sensible, and comprehensive ticket acknowledges frankly and with a good grace the twofold nature of the Berlin pilgrims, corporeal and spiritual, and gives intelligence suited to their wants in both capaci-

ing ties ; it is a folded map of Berlin, contain- 011 the back " all the necessary intor- " mation as to the subject-matter of every " day's conference, the names of the speak- " ers, preachers, and religious institutions " of the city, and an indication where " the members can best meet lor refreshthese gentlemen meet in the " Garnison þÿ ment and mutual intercourse." Well, Kirche," which is " provided with ail " ample carpeted platform" for the occasion, the 100th Psalm is sung, Pastor Kuntzel opens the proceedings with " an " eloquent prayer, which elicits the excla- " mation from some of the audience, ' He " prays like Spurgeon !' " There is then a " and Christian union." There is a se- great ' deal of talk about brotherly " love" " ries of greetings" and religious salutations, as c ne minister is introduced to another minister, as Wesleyan Methodist shakes hands with an Episcopalian Methodist, and an English Calvinist with a French Calvinist. Lastly, a special train conveys 900 members of the Alliance to Potsdam, where " they find abundant refreshment and am- " " rococo pie attendance saloons." There is a shout of awaiting them in the " Hoch !" and " Hurrah !" as His Prussian Majesty enters. The enthusiasm reaches its height, and when Sir Culling the whole crowd of English visitors, " en- Eardley and the English deputation, with " closed the group of King, Chamberlains, " and " like Adjutants a cluster of bees, the Queen, from in one dense hot mass, " whose recollection the events of 1848

" were not yet effaced, gave evident signs fect of confinement within " a dense mass " of apprehension " But, though the ef- " like a cluster of bees" is sometimes serious, it is needless to say that this pressure was not for any hostile purpose, but only for a demonstration of the warmest affection. Even death itself could have been hardly otherwise than blissful under such circumstances, for, though people generally object to being killed with kindness, as much as to any other way of being killed, still the embrace of the Evangelical Alliance must be allowed to have something

» tr & n o. i þÿ v I transcendental, heavenly, and Elysian about it. Sidney Smith was, indeed, ungallant enough to describe the reward which he received for a most welcome piece of news and a most kind act of patronage as " being " " enveloped women." But suffocation by the Evan- in the embraces of two fat gelical Alliance would have been in itself an apotheosis. The soul of Tom Bowling could hardly have gone aloft under happier circumstances than under the affectionate, downy, and fragrant pressure of so many dozen spiritual pillows comfortably and softly squeezing the luckiest of martyrs into eternity. We have no fault, we say, to find with all this enthusiasm. We do not wish to' speak lightly of the gift of " praying like Spurgeon," and we are far too much " awed " by black coats and white the solemn and august army of 900 cravats marshalled " according to nationalities" to give vent to any levity on the occasion, even supposing we were inclined to do so. But we cannot help at the same time asking the question þÿ What is all this about ? What is the object of it all ? Some people see a great object in all this. Mr. Wright, the American Minister at Berlin, who calls the Evangelical Alliance " Our Christ our Lord, our Bible," of course sees a great work done at these Conferences, anil we suppose that all who attend at them also see a great work dune at them. They appear to be satisfied, and more than satisfied. They come to Berlin with sanguine expectations, and they go away with those ex-

pectations completely fulfilled. They are set up spiritually for the next year, and feel that a great victory has been won over the Powers of Darkness. Something, then, has been done on the occasion. What is it? A number of gentlemen speak about brotherly love and charity " " greet" each other, shake hands, and meet for mutual intercourse and refreshment." All this is perfectly unobjectionable, and very proper. Our only difficulty is, why people should go to Berlin to do it. Cannot they preach love and charity at their own homes ? Do we need the Conferences at Berlin to tell us that brotherly love and charity and Christian union are very good things ? We know that well enough ; the difficulty is in the matter of practice. The Christian world is unhappily rather defective in the practice of these virtues. Will the Conferences at Berlin help to this practical result? Will one. single veneinous Christian in Germany, France, England, or America bite or sting any the less because the Evangelical Alliance praises brotherly love ? Will he dip his pen a bit the less in gall when he attacks an adversary be- cause " 900 men in black coats and white " according to their nationalities "cravats have been marshalled at Berlin ?" This Evangelical Alliance has no definite or tangible object, that we see. If it wanted to break up all existing boundaries and lines of demarcation that separate one Protestant from another þÿ if it aimed at the annihilation of the English Church, and the

Scotch Church, and all Dissenting denominations, and the final absorption of all these separate bodies of Protestants in itself, as one grand centreþÿ this would be an extravagantly chimerical object, but still it would be a tangible one. The whole professed object, however, of the Evangelical Alliance as now constituted, is that Protestants, retaining their present distinctions, and going on exactly as they do now, as so many sepq/ate and independent bodies, should be annually exhorted to love one another. What is the particular use of this ? This is done one year at Edinburgh, another at Paris, another at Berlin. What is the difference between something said at Edinburgh and exactly the same thing said

at Berlin ? The lesson is the same, the people who preach it are the same, everything is the same except the place, which is Edinburgh one year, and Berlin another. What need is there of an Association to preach this sermon, and still more of a nomad Association ? Why all this expense in steamers and railway tickets? We cannot see the use of all this trouble and outlay, the fabric of a formal Association and the pomp of Conferences, in order to teach men a very plain lesson which they knowwell enough already, and are not a bit the more likely to practise.

An Extraordinary Affair. þÿ A reward has been offered under the following cir cumstances : þÿ On Tuesday, the 1st Sept., a small box, covered with brown paper, and directed to Mr. Bennett, surgeon, the Square, Wilton, was delivered to Mrs. Ware, the Wilton carrier, near the Shoulder of Mutton Inn, Salisbury, by a boy about 14 years of age, dressed in a short jacket, trousers, and cap. BELGIUM. THE NEW MINISTRY. The Belgian Cabinet is now reconstituted as follows : þÿ Interiorþÿ M. Charles Rogier. Finance þÿ M. Frere-Orban. Justice þÿ M. Tesch. Foreign Affairs þÿ Baron de Vriere. War þÿ General Berten. M. Partoes, Secretary-General in the Department of Public Works, is intrusted provisionally remain a few weeks. with the direction of that department. The two Chambers met on Tuesday, according to the terms of the constitution. At 1 þÿo clock the members of the Chamber of Representatives assembled in their usual place of session. The new Ministers, M. Rogier, M. Frere-Orban, Baron de Vriere, and so Ministerial bench. The tribunes and M. Tesch, took their places on the and the reserved places were fully occupied. The galleries were also tilled by a large crowd of persons, amongst whom was a large number of elegantly attired ladies. In of the Palace and its neighbourhood congregated an immense assemblage of the public, through which a passage could only be made with the greatest difficulty. The sentinals in and around the Chambers were doubled. At a quarter past 1 the session of the Chambers was opened in the absence of the King or a Royal speech. The Assembly was about to commence with the verification of the powers of the newly elected members, when M. Rogier, Minister of the Interior, ascended the tribune and read a Royal decree adjourning the i Chambers. Alter the announcement of his Royal decree, cries of þÿ Vive the seance terminated amid le lioi þÿ! notwithstanding

the claims of M. Dumortier, a leading member of the clerical party, to be heard, the hon. representative loudly contending that the decree of adjournment could not properly be read until after the formal constitution of the burenu of the Chamber. The i Royal decree for the adjournment of the Chambers was read afterwards to the Senate, which immediately separated. The Free-traders of Belgium are much elated at the change of Ministry, believing that their principles will now gain immense strength by the accession to office of many of their avowed friends. They have recently held four large meetings in furtherance of customs reform in different parts of the country, viz., at Antwerp, St. Nicolas, Bruges, and Courtrai, and are organizing a system of agitation all over the country.

At a special meeting of the Vestry of St. þÿPaul s Church, Frederiksted, convened at the Rectory, on the 20th November, the following Preamble audResolutions, relating to the recent death of the late Right Reverend Daniel Date ward Davis, D.D., Lord Bishop of þÿ adopted That Antigua, were unanimously Whereas þÿ The English parishes in this Island, although not situated in the Diocese Proper of Antigua, and therefore having no claim upon the time, and attention of its Bishop, are nevertheless indebted to his kindness, for all the Episcopal privilges which they have enjoyed during the last fifteen y ears þÿ among which may be mentioned, the consecration of our churches, and the confirmation of many hundreds of our people þÿ and, Whereas þÿ The Vestry of this Church are deeply inipressedj with the propriety of giving some public expression of their gratitude to the late Right Revd. Bishop for these long continued and valuable services to this congregation, as well as of their heartfelt regret for the loss which they have sustained bv his death þÿ Therefore it is hereby Resolved That this Vestry are deeply seu- þÿ sible that in the death of Bishop Davis, our Parish has#sustnincd the loss of a kind, and efficient friend, of whose many highly appreciated visitations and services they will ever cherish a most grateful remembrance. Resolved þÿ That this parish sympathises sincerely with the Clergy and Laity of the Diocese of Antigua in the sad bereavment which the inscrutable

wisdom of the Almighty has sent upon . them, and in common with them, great- ly deplores the loss of their much esteemed Bishop. Resolved þÿ That in testimony of our regret, and as a slight tribute of our respect, for the memory of the departed Bishop, our church be dressed in black, until the Festival of Christmas. Resolved þÿ That these resolutions be read to the congregation by the Rector, from the Chancel, on Sunday next ; and be entered together with the minutes of this meeting, into the Parish Records. .(no. C. DuBois, R. F. Smith, ) Chairman. Q. J. Mudie, ) Vestry and Warden.

Under tho head of þÿ Summary for Home þÿReaders, the Demerara Royal Gazelle supplies the following communication, addressed by the West India Committee iu London to the Lieut. - Governor of British Guiana : þÿ West India Committee, Walbrook House, ) London, October 16, 1857. j Sir, þÿ 1 am instructed by the West India Committee to communicate with ycur Excellency on a subject of great importanoe to the West India Colonies. When the present unhappy struggle in India is brought to a close, and British supremacy once more firmly established, there will be, it is anticipated, a very considerable number of natives of whom it will be requisite to make a severe exam' pie, short of the punishment of death. This may be dono by transporting them for life to a distant country, and the West India Colonies have been; indicated as localities where they

might easily be separated into small parties, and where their labour would be beneficial. A preliminary conference has already taken place with some of the leading Directors of the East India Company, and the principal proprie-

have been consulted. There is a general desire that the experiment should be tried, but as it may be attended with j risk to the colonies whilst its success must at any j rate be doubtful, it is considered that the expense of deportation should be borne by the East India Company. However this may be, the task of receiving aud employing the exiles and of preventing their escape will necessarily fall upon the West Indies. An act of the Imperial Parliament is necessary for enabling the East India Company to transport beyond the limits of their charter, and this oanuot be obtained before the Spring, so that there is suffieient, time for a well digested definite plan, which may at the proper moment be laid before Her þÿMajesty Government. s As this class of mutineers will consist of those whose offences have been most venial, who have dron, they will afford shelter and support to our j in fact been led or forced away by others rather than active in the revolt, it is considered that the transportation should, if possible, be their only whatever source maintained, form parts of the ! punishment, that they should be regarded as defences of the empire, aud it will be necessary I exiles rather than convicts, and allowed to earn

burse the colony for any expenses and possibly I pay for the passage of their wives aud children. They will therefore probably be apprenticed ou various estates for a term of years, in the same manner as free emigrants, and those wbo may prove refractory and unmanageable may be emþÿp oyedby government in penal gangs. The deductions from their wages and the inability to return, may probably nake a sufficient distinction between the exiles and free immiþÿ but this will be for your careful consideration. It seems probable that the families of many might accompany them, aDd I need not call your attention to the importance of this, with reference to a due proportion of the sexes. Should your Excellency think well of this attempt, to remedy the deficiency of population in the West Indies, you are respectfully invited to inform me. « How many Indians your colony is willing to take ? What provisions you can make for their recepi tion, and what notice youwill require? Whether your existing laws will give you sufi ficient control over them, or whether it will be neoessary to insert clauses for this purpose in the j Act which will enable the transportation to be j carried out. I have the honor to be, Sir, Your most obedient Servant, STEPHEN CAVE Deputy Chairman To His Exoellenoy William Walker, Lieut.-Governor, &c. &c &c., British Guiana. The above communication has likewise been forwarded to the several Governors of the British Islands.

This he considers, in the first place and oi highest impo t:it>i e, to be, that the Royal laws and ordinances are obeyed, and in this respect he believes that it is , in the well-understood Interest of the whole that the screw be kept as tight as the law demands. With regard to the question on the fixing of the average gauge of rum puncheons complained ofþÿ the ordinances determine a certain per cent duty for every Gallon exported, and it is therefore incumbent on the Inspector to take care that , the þÿState þÿtreasury s r s ight, in this as well as in ( every other direction where th qti- stion has reference to the revenues of this duty department, be fully secured. the present article gives the honored þÿ Candour right when be says that the loss it may ocoasion to the single producer or exporter þÿ is a pitiful paltry, þÿchcese-paring-affair.
