The address to His Excellency the Governor on the subject of tho proposed new duties on the produce of this Island, when imported into Denmark, was delivered on Thursday last at Dane Garden, numerously signed. We understand that His Excellency the Governor promised to use his utmost endeavours to secure a 1 fair consideration of the important matters in question, and to forward it to the home government as soon as possible. As several of the resolutions agreed on at the meeting have bcon more fully explained in the address, our readers may approve of our printing below a translation from the original Danish, forwarded to us for publication. The undersigned planters and merchants of St. Croix tuke the liberty to address your Excellency respecting the project fora new tariff of customs lately emanated from a superior authority in Copenhagen, þÿ as far

as the said projected tariff tends materially to alter the conditions under which our produce, especially sugar, has heretofore been imported to the lnothercountry, and indeed to deal therewith as with loreign produce. We have not before us any official publication concerning the intended new tariff regulations affecting so powerfully the interests of this island, but from the statements of the Copenhagen press there can be no doubt on the matter ; and the more we regret, that the authority has not þÿ allowed to our industry the same opportunity to attend to its rather considerable interest, as has been offered to other branches of industry in the mothercountry more or less affected by the changes proposed. Having no information whether it is not intended to lay the new tariff before the imperial council in its approaching session, we would not be justified in postponing for the expected meeting of the Colonial Council our present request, that your Excellency will represent our just claims td the Minister in charge of these affairs. In conformity with resolutions agreed on at two public meetings, at which the present business has been considered, we beg first testate with regird to the principle to be acted on in dealing with such questions affecting this colony, that acknowledging unreservedly the right of the Legislature to alter the present imposts on the produce of the island, we at the same time deprecate and protest against any public act or fiscal regulation, implying that the

inhabitants of this island are not entitled within tbe extent of the Danish monarchy to the same regard and the same at least negative protection of their industry, which the legislature acknowledges to be due to or does practically grant to the inhabitants of the mothercountry mid ot its other colonies. The people of this island trust and confide, that neither fiscal theories nor local and þÿtrades interests will be considered by the Danish Government, the legislative assembly and the Danish people to warrant any new enactment, tending to deal with the agricultural produce ot this Danish island as with foreign produce, to be taxed on its importation to Denmark exclusively with a view to realize the highest obtainable customs-revenue therefrom. That the sugar and ruin produced in St. Croix are brought into the ports of the mothercountry beyond the sea docs not ' alter the real nature of the present impost thereon, as an inland þÿ or excise duty; there has not been brought forward any reasonable cause to alter or to abolish the small and long established difference between that duty and the import duty on foreign muscovadoes, amounting to about on ; Kixdollar pr. 1001b. We cannot understand, on what principle it is inf.< i led to levy foreign duty on our sugars in Denmark, when both under tbe present tariff and under the projected new tariff other domestic branches of nidusj try, some of them not very important, are protected to some extent ; the more so, as any industry established within the mothercountry enjoys one essential advantage against importations from foreign places, say with regard to the cost of transport ; but the produce of this colony of course enjoys no such advantage.

Nor are we aware of any modern state I ' colonies in this manner. The nature of the question does not dispense from considerations of' equity ; and it ought not to be overlooked, that the British West India colonies have gone through the disturbances of emancipation much earlier, have received from their rnothercountry a larger amount of compensation and been otherwise indemnified ; that they have been powerfully assisted by government to obtain foreign laborers; that generally they do not pay taxes to the British treasury, which however defrays the salaries of the superior authorities and all the expense of the military establishments in the colonies. The Danish islands have in most respects been placed under far less favorable conditions ; and the cane cultivation of 8t. Croix, which has been suffering ever since emancipation, notwithstanding energetic and continued exertions of the planters, and has not yet been able to obtain foreign laborers, does already bear a much heavier taxation, than that of any other colony in the West- ,

indies. Besides the assimilation of the duty on St. Croix and foreign muscovadoes, the j new tariff also proposes to admit foreign refined or half refined sugars, when crushed j or otherwise pulverized, at the same duty as muscovadoes, reserving for a few years | u nominal difference in favor of our inuscovadoes (which at present pay only about J , of the duty on crushed refined). This innovation we consider to be so momentous, so threatening, under all the circumstances, to our commercial relations with the rnothercountry, that in the 1 event of this or any similar measure being carried, we should be fairly entitled to claim as an act of common justice, that the impost on our sugars now levied in Den- ; mark as import-duty be abolished, and that they be hereafter, like any other d finish produce, admitted free of duty. Bagger Esqr., Royal Book-keeper. o From the Weekly Dispatch. \ The latest telegrams i'rom Malta tell us that the anticipations of this journal are thoroughly fulfilled, or rather outgone, for the success of Colonel Greathed and the column detached southwards from Delhi is more triumphant than any one could have a right to expect. Looking at the dates and at the map, comparing the distances with the usual rate of marching in India and especially where the ground is occupied or disputed by an enemy, we can hardly trust to the calculation that he would reach Luckuow by the 30th of October, having arrived at Agra on the 10th, and subsequently defeated new assailants in that quarter, supposed to be the Gwalior and Indoor contingents. What this officer and his column of 3,000 have already been able to achieve, as ascertained in Calcutta, roves how complete was the rout of the rebels in Delhi, and to what little effect the yet considerable Sepoy force which certainly escaped from that capital lias been enable to rally. Battles have been fought at Bolundshuhur and at Allyghur, hut the ground has been fairly cleared as the column advanced. Agra has not only been delivered from the force already threatening it, but preserved from new foes, the contingents once in our pay, that had forced Holkar aud Sciudiali to act on the defensive, if

not to temporize ; and if the 300 miles from Agra to Cawnpoor can be covered in 19 or 20 days, we may indeed be sure that the strength of the revolt is hopelessly broken, and that, if any great action in the field is to precede the close of the war, the whole issue will be brought on at Lucknow, where llavelook with 1,500 men has been jutted against 50,000 rebels. He is now seriously reinforced, though he yet delays to risk the women and children by a march. Outram, at Cawnpoor, has also considerable additions to his strength, and Greathed will be advancing almost along Outram's line, or a little to the north of m to help in bringing the main body of the rebels to their last stand. It is not too much to say that this gives proof of our marked and of course our increasing superiority. Hearing that there were large forces such as ILivelock could only meet on the defensive at Luckuow itself, knowing that the jrebel regiments dislodged from Delhi would naturally converge to this reserve of Lucknow besiegers, beaten indeed, but not driven from its scene of action, we expected a far more obstinate ami wearying contest in driving in the mass to the field on which it must accept decisive battle. We shall rejoice indeed to hear that the 30th of October found the united British forces aVrayed against the Oude army of the rebels, and we will not waste a line in speculating on the result. Our readers will see the welcome list of ships and regiments arriving at Calcutta, or marked, as on their way to it, at Point de

Galle, as well as mustering at Madras. Other vessels must be near Kurrachee and Bombay on the western coast. Five thousand men seem almost enough to make India sure, and these are already landed at Calcutta. We have fortunately to multiply this number by 6 or 7 within a very few weeks, iu estimating all the troops that, are to disembark at the various points. Such drawback as exists in the intelligence is found in the danger of Sanger, and

in the bad spirit rising at Hyderabad in Nizam's dominion. This mutinous disposition appears to us to be confirmed by the order given at Calcutta to the Caledonia to return south to Masuliputam, and disembark her troops there. If we now regret the perversity of any new foes, without denying the injury they may inflict, our sorrow is not a little for their own sake aud for the misery into which they must drag every accomplice, willing or forced. The defection of Maun Singh must be on some purely personal ground. He can hardly reckon loss to us from our victor' at Delhi The most convincing corroboration of the good news is in the tact thai the. revenue is being brought in very rapidly. This is the true Eastern propitiation of the conqueror. It would have been withheld if there had been a chance of saving it, or if a stronger antagonistic power were at all likely hereafter to demand it. To Saugor we pointed when last writing on this most interesting subject. The place is, as nearly as possible, in the centre of the peninsula, and, therefore, more out of reach from the greater depots of our strength than almost any other. A painful suspense much attach to the fate of its European inhabitants until the unquestioned success of our arms in every direction strikes panic into the hearts of all our enemies ; and, for the sake of those penned up in every isolated garrison, we must therefore pray that success may be speedily pushed on to an indisputable catastrophe, and be grateful
to those incomparable soldiers who are acting O such wonders of celerity J as well as of valour.

Private letters received here from Mexico afford a sort of clue to the political movements at present agitating that republic. Of one thing these letters assure us, and that is, that Commonfort will not be able to sustain himself. Only the men in office are paid, whilst all other claims upon the administration are allowed to go unsatisfied. A state of things like this cannot long continue. There were some hopes that Commonfort would succeed in making a treaty with Mr. Forsyth, by which the treasury of the United States would aid Mexico ; but under existing circumstances, the arrangement is not likely to be made, and the Congress, you will perceive, while giving extraordinary powers to Commonfort withhold sanction to the alienation of Mexican territory. Left alone, Mexico must necessarily fall into the hands of the United States. The conclusion is a self-evident one. There lias been frequent allusion from time to time to the return of General Santa Anna, but that disinterested and incorruptible patriot will not coine to the aid of his country again unless strongly invited. The letters to which I refer do not hesitate to insinuate that General Cortez, detained at the national capital, is actually negotiating with Commontbrt terms for the return of Gene-

LET VERY WELL ALONE. Frederiksted ism December 1857. To the Editor of the Avis, Dear Sir, I recollect reading, sotne years ago, a Story in an English Periodical, with the above Motto,

had Let-u acrm-cd of murder. The trial which gave an accouut of the trial of a man who . which created great interest and exeltt'Ui "t u the neighbouihuod where the occurrence jk place ; and, as may well be supposed the comes; profession it is to strive to make the worse between the Gentlemen of the long-robe, whose '' appear the better cause," called forth a great di.-play of legal ability and forensic eloquence, as such a momentous occasion always does produce, on the part of the leading C nuisel engaged on both sides. The public mind was held iu a painful state of tension during the progress of the trial, as fact after fact was being developed, and which came out so strongly against the Prisoner at the Bar as to carry conviction of his Guilt to the minds of the entire multitude assembled in and about the Court House to witness the trial Not the smallest doubt was entertained by any one present of the Jury's bringing in a verdict of guilty against the accused. But the glorious uncertainty of the law interposed in Ills favor, and to the amazement of the whole community he was acquitted þÿ upon what ground, at this distance of time I cannot exactly rememli r þÿ but he was acquitted however, very probably by some trifling flaw in the indictment, or by one of those strange paradoxes which sometimes occur iu law proceedings. The law could not reach him and he left the Dock, it is true, with a verdict in his favor þÿ the law acquitted him ; but not so the public þÿ no quibble, subterfuge, or legal vagary,

could shake the conviction which plain unvarnished truth had established in the public mind, and the sequel proved its correct ness Emboldened by bis success and uot content with his miraculous escape from the punishment duo to his crime (as was afterwards proved,) he had the imprudent temerity to institute a prosecution against his accusers for defamation of character, and demanded heavy damages for the injury done his fair-fame. Bui justice does not always sleep ; the prosecution brought on a re-investigation of the case ; new evidence was produced þÿ he was tried ; found þÿguilty and was hanged ! The above brief outline of a story which so strongly illustrates the prudence and wisdom which men would often show by the observance of the motto hero þÿquoted let very well alone þÿ was brought to my remembrance by leading your notice iu the Avis, the other day, that an action had been entered against that Journal by Mr. Koefoed, Manager of Enfield Green Estate, in consequence of your having reported the proceedings in a Police suit instituted against Lnm. on the complaint of Mr. John Elliott, for the alledged Bribery of a labourer named Maliouy and bis family, who resided on Mr. Elliott's Estate ; a oase to which the moral of this story might not bo very inaptly applied By tho Police decision suflLieut direct evidence it seems could not be produced, according to the requirements of law, to prove the case one of Bribery. It was not denied, however, that the amount of

40$ was paid to Mahouy as stated þÿ no, this could not be denied þÿ but tho stale, shallow, mean subterfuge, now so much in fashion on such occasions, of a loan was fallen back upou. It would app ar that the overflowing beuevolent feelings of Mr Koefoed wanted vent, so poor Mahouy was considered a worthy recipient, the more especially as he was a sort of Patriarch and had some 6 able people comprising his family, all of whom no doubt would be welcome, iu addition to this disinteres'ed generosity, to locate themselves on Estate Enfield Green, and Mr. Elliott with whom they were quite content to remain, as a natural cousequence " was to be deprived of their services. But, tell it not in Gath" þÿ mum's the word, or the strong arm of the law will be down upon you. So then it would appear all these sort of proceedings are to be considered fair and honorable among men ! O lemporo, O mores. Oh how convenient this word Loan has become of late years to many in thi Island, and what mean dirty tricks it serves to cover, and too often, I fear, enables men to escape the just penalty due to their offences. But Mahony it appears did not avail himself of the rare cliauce thus invitingly opened to liira, by so generous a subsidy (this is a better word than Loan þÿ the word has become odious) of obtaining a residence ou the south side þÿ and besides, Ah 1 that was the unkiudest cut of all and poor he let tiie cat out of the bag þÿ to his Master. Mahony should feel þÿit and in order to carry out

the fnrce still further, I understand Mahony has been sued iu this town for the repayment of this money, which he did not seek for, but which on the contrary was in a manner thrust upon him--from purs disinterested kindness of þÿcourse this

line of proceeding, being considered necessary, I presu'u to show that it was a loan, for by the Police proceedings published it will be perceived the d irties were so .cunning as to give the matter the ipp'aranoe of an ordinary business transaction, and a Mortgage was accordingly taken in Maboappear ny's Cart and from to me Pony. Now, Mr. Editor, it does a due consideration of all the facts of this case before the public, that Mr. Koefoed would have acted wisely as far as can gathered from the Police proceedings, in ' let- be ting very well þÿalone" the lucky decision which be obtained, by quietly slinking and behind congratulating himself at the same time on his escaping so well, aud I dare say he may think so too before all's over. You may be prosecuted, and you may be hned also, and Mahony s Pony aud Cart may be sold, but the public can uot be blinded by dust ; not all the water in the sea will suffice to cleanse this affair of its real character in the public mind If the object of the prosecution be to scare and mulct you for doing that which in all enlightened communities it would be considered you had perfect right to do as a public Journalist, a matter which i. e. to give seriously concerned the public will be I believe expression to public opinion in interest, I can safely assert Mr Koefoed signally owe it to themselves disappointed iu his to expectations. in The public support you your position as Editor, and not allow you to suffer the smallest pecuniary loss for the manly and correct

LAUNCHING THE LEVIATHAN. On Saturday morning a third attempt was made to move this gigantic vessel, which, we are happy to say, was eminently successful, and resulted in the Leviathan being gradually lowered down the launching ways some 25 feet, in a slow and beautifully regular manner. The whole distance was accomplished without any accident or delay worth speaking of, and throughout the entire day the advance of the ship was regulated according as Mr. Brunnel thought fit with as much ease and certainty as if the vessel had been a little cutter, instead of a ponderous structure of irou weighing upwards of 12,000 tons. Indeed every inch which the colossus advanced gave fresh cause for admiring the forethought and perfect accuracy with which all the mechanical details connected with her launching have bean arranged, in spite of the novelty of the undertaking and the utter absence of all ordinary rules for guidance. þÿ London Times.

ATTEMPTED MUTINY IN THE BOMBAY ARMY. The fiiimbiii/ Times publishes the following letters describing the suppression of an alarming outbreak at Kurrachee : þÿ Kurracliee, 14th September. You will be sorry to learn that the 21st Regiment Native Infantry was disarmed here last night at 12 p.m., in consequence of information given to Major þÿM Grigor by two subalnl.tTs of bis regiment, las; night at half-past 1 1, that the whole of the regiment had arranged to loot the treasury, arsenal, magazine and camp bazaar, at 12 p.m. Major M Grcgor immediately assembled his officers, and then rode to the 2nd Europeans, of whom four companies are here at present, and then to the artillery, and got them ready. Measures were taken to get the European ladies of the station assembled at the inesshouse of the 2nd Europeans. The men of the 2nd Europeans and the Artillery were marched to the lines of the 21st, and just as they were coming near a bugle was sounded from the 21st Native Infantry, for the men to assemble, as arranged by them, to loot the station. They were surprised to find themselves surrounded by the men of the 2nd and the Artillery, and ordered to pile arms, which they did, after which the lines were searched, and it is reported a very large number of swords, cutlasses and hatchets (very sharp) were found, and many of the muskets were ready loaded. It is nowfound that 2d of the men of the 21st ran away yesterday with their muskets, &c. The police have gone in search of them.

September ISth. The accounts given by the local papers about the attempted mutiny and disarming of the 21st Native Infantry at this station, will, if extracted in your paper, give your readers an idea ot how we were disturbed last Sunday night and Monday morning, so that I need not dw-ell lengthily on the matter. Suffice it, that between 11 and 12 þÿo clock, the 3rd Troop Horse Artillery, the new field battery, and the head-quarters ot the 2nd Europeans were out, aud reached the lines ol
tempt of an outbreak. They were disarmed without a single shot being fired on that is possible 1 either side, about 28 men deserted the line-

with their muskets. The capturing of these men was left to the Kurrachee police who right well performed their work, bringing them in, fours and fives at a time. Niue prisoners were brought ih to-day, with three heads, the possessors having opposed resistance to the police, who felled them. This, 1 believe, closes the list ol deserters. That the intended mutineers have little sympathy from the Scindians is proved by the fact of one of the deserters having been brought in by some Beloocheos, who disarmed him fearlessly, although he discharged his musket at one of them, but without injuring him. The ten men who were first captured were tried by court-martial, and executed yesterday evening, seven being hanged and three blown from guns. The whole of the troops were ordered out to witness the spectacle. The scalfold has been taken down to-day, so that we do not know what the authorities intend doing with the remaining deserters ; but it is believed that every one will be executed, as important disclosures of matured plans to destroy the European inhabitants have been made to the court. The decision shown by the General in executing these men so soon is highly lauded ; it has carried terror to the hearts of the natives. We have soldiers patrolling the streets throughout the night since Monday; and last night particularly, pickets from the troop were galloping up and down. A number of ollicers also formed processions, and went about camp. The guard of the treasury at the cutcherry has been entrust-

The New York Post-Okfice. þÿ A correspondent of the Washington States relates some interesting facts concerning the immense business transacted at the New York Post-office. The weight of the Southern mail, on a single day, is over ten thousand pounds ! þÿ or more than five tons. The weight of the mail forwarded by the Erie road is over sixteen thousand pounds þÿ or more than eight tons þÿ that sent by the Hudson river over four tons in weight. Tiie weight of the entire mails forwarded on one day of last week was over forty thousand pounds þÿ or more than twenty tons. There is now employed in the Postoffice of New þÿY ork, a clerk who has been there forty years. Thirty-five years ago this clerk carried the entire Southern mail daily, under his arm, across the river then Jersey City. That mail, which could to be tied up in a handkerchief, now weighs some five or six tons each day, and has to be transported from the Post-office in heavy wagons, making several loads. If the increase of the mails may be regarded as an index of the general growth and progress of the country in all that adds to the prosperity of the nation, then truly, we are a progressive people.

( From the Weekly Despatch, October 25.) THE SUPPOSED MURDER AND MUTILATION.

All doubts at to thu safety of Mr. Patterson, from Australia, have been removed by the receipt of a communication by Mr. Superintendent Darkin, stating that he is alive and well. There seems to be a growing feeling in the minds of the officers who have been entrusted with th inquiry into this mysterious affair that a hoax has been perpetrated, and that all probabilities of tracing the persons who have committed it are at an end It was stated in the Dispatch of Sunday last, that some of the most experienced men in the City detective force had expressed an opinion privately that no murder had been committed, and the officers of the metropolitan force are ooming to the same conclusion. At all events, they have now no clue whatever Irom which there is any hope of an identification of the carpet-bag, the woman who carritd it on the bridge, or the clothes of the deceased man ; or of a discovery of the remainder of the hody, of which the bones now lying at Bow-street station formed a part. From a communication made to the Police on Wednesday morning it appears some sensation was created at. Barneson Tuesday night by the discoverv of the portion of a human body which was floating in the Thames. On its being taken on shore it wns examined by Dr. Pulling, who found that it was the thigh of a male person, which had been subjected to some chemical process. Unfortuuately, however, this discovery will lead to no practical result in connection with the present allcdged murder, as both thighs of

the mangled body found on the buttress of Waterloo-bridge are amongst the remains at tho station. The police have at length found that the exhibition of the clothes drew together many hundreds of persons, who were prompted merely by idle curiosity, and that the crowds which daily flocked to inspect them proved a serious obstacle to the transaction of the ordinary business of the day. On Wednesday morning, therefore, the public were not admitted, but the clothes are still at the station, and any one may see them who really has any idea that he may be able to give information to the police It is necessary to mention this oircumstanoc, because statements of the most absurd and mis-leading character have appeared, to the effect that the clothes have been sent for a provincial tour, and that afterwards they are to be transmitted to foreign countries and to the United States. A man who is well known to all the toll-takers at Waterloo-bridge, made a statement to tho polioc to the effect that, having read the accounts in tho papers of the horrible murder, he thought he might be enabled to give such information as would materially assist the police in their endeavours to unravel the mystery whioh surrounds the case, and lead to the apprehension of tho femalo who took the bag on the bridge on the night prior to the discovery. He states most positively that on the night alluded to, before he crossed over Waterloo-bridge, as he always did two or three times a day, he went to the turnstile and proceeded to light his pipo

at the gas-lamp, and, while doing so, a woman came up with a carpet-bag and a paper parcel. He heard a portion of the conversation that took place between the woman and Errington, but. of course took no notice of the matter until he heard of the disoovery. He, however, had a clear and distinct view of her features, and expresses his ability to ' swear to her out of a þÿthousand, for, besides her peculiar cast of features, there

ST IU I U li S was a þÿ þÿmole on her right cheek, which will render identification doubly sure. Shortly after 11 þÿo clock on Wednesday night Superintendent Darkin, accompanied by Inspector Mackenzie aud a number of the Thames police, repaired to Waterloo-bridge for the purpose of making experiments with a bag similar to that in which the remains of the murdered man were found. The tide was at the same height as on the night of the murder. The carpet-bag used which weighed exactly 301b. 'the precise weight of the bag containing the remains) was lifted on the parapet and from thence swung over tbe second parapet. The first parapet is nearly two feet wide, and the second about two feet six. It will be seen, therefore, that any person standing on the stone seat of the recess, and holding the bag at þÿarm l s ength, so as to clear both parapets, must have been possessed not only of considerable physical power, but of a steady hand, and more than ordinary nerve. The place from whioh the bag was lowered was as nearly as possible tho centre of the recess. As soun as the bag cl(red the second parapet, 20 yards of rope were payed out as fast as possible, aud alter the lapse of a lew seconds the bag was found to rest firmly upon tho buttress. The experiment was tried a second time with similar results. The police arc satisfied that the bag could not have been deposited on the buttress by any person in a boat on the river beneath, as the tide runs so strong past the buttress that no boat could have

been brought up so as to lodge a burden on it. Tho strength required for lowering the bag, so as to clear the parapet of the bridge, would warrant the assumption that the woman was assisted by some person who met her in the recess, and decamped the moment the bag was lowered. from OCR OWN REPORTER. All tho inquiries made by the police duriug the past week have failed to elicit any fresh information upon the subject of this offence, and tbe general impression now is, even among a good many of tho police themselves, that it amounts to no more than a medical þÿstudent hoax, s and that there is an entire absence of any evidence to show that a murder has been committed. It has been already urged, in support of this hypothesis, that the mere fact of tbe bones having been divided in an unscientific manner was not in any way conclusive of the fact that the act was committed by persons unacquuiDtcd with tbe science of anatomy, because it was evident that the parties who were concerned in the proceeding would have adopted this as the readiest mode of throwing the police and others off the scent, as if the limbs had been separated at the joints in the manner they would have been by an anatomist, the suggestion of a murder having been committed would have been at ouce rendered doubtful, and it was quite os easy for them to be hacked asunder and thus further the original object of deceiving and greatly alarming the public. There does not at present appear to be the slightest foundation for a great number of

the absurd and extravagant statements that have been made public upon the subject of this supposed horrible murder and mutilation ; but one fact, namely, the alleged pickling or salting of the remains, upon which great stress has been laid, is confirmatory of the views that a murder bad been oommitted, would seem to those at all acquainted with tbe course of proceedings in hospitals, and the mode in which students in anatomy carry on these studies, to be conclusive of tho fact that these remains were brought irom some 8uch establishment, and that tho theory of the body having been salted to preserve it from decomposition, until an opportunity should be afforded to make away with it, is perfectly ridiculous, and the circumstance of the remains having

apparently been placed in pickle of some description, can be explained in a much more simple manner. It is well known that in the cour-e of a medical þÿstudent s practice in anatomy he has to dissect a leg, an arm, or a thigh as the case may be, his attention being directed to one particular portion of the human frame, and the dissection or examination may, according to the diligence of the pupil, be extended over a very considerable period, and, during tbe intervals, the limb, or other portions of the body, is always placed in a receptacle filled with brine adapted to the purpose, tbe part being still equally eligible for the purposes of anatomical examination, and the danger and nuisance of decomposition bein ' avoided This would appear to be a much more satisfactory explanation of the remains found in tho carpet-bag having teen þÿ þÿpickled in tiiis manner, than that tbe person or persons who were supposed to have been guilty of a most horrible crime, and who might at once, clearly, if they had been so minded, have made off, and evaded detection, should have resorted to such extraordinary and elaborate means to conceal the crime. It should also be remembered that (hero is no conclusive evidence that the bones and other portions of the human body found in the carpet-bag ever belonged to the same living in dividual, and the facility with which mortal remains of this description enn be obtained in hospitals and other publio ins'itulions of that kind, would render it a matter of no difficulty to obtain
such portions as were found in the carpet-bag, the discovery of which has caused so much excitement upon the supposition that a barbarous murder had been committed

From the Weekly Dispatch FRANCE. The Moniteur contains a report, addressed to the Emperor by M. Magne, relative to the budget for 1858. There is an excess in the reveuues of 43 millions of francs : 10 millions of which are applied to the liquidation of the debt. The financial review of the country is of an extremely favourable character. The reduction of the floating debt is assured, and all loans paid. The Patrie announces that official negotiations are going on between Fiance and England for i an exchange of territory in India. It is proposed that France should give up her possessions in Chaudernagor to England, receiving, as an equivalent, a portion of territory near Pondecherry, which is the centre of the French colonies in India. ,

BELGIUM. Letters from Brussels bring news of extraordinary success obtained by the Liberal party in the communal elections of Oct. 27. The Liberals have been equally triumphant at Ghent and Antwerp The Ministry is alarmed at the result of the elections, which was not expected to be so very decided

CHRISTIA.N3TED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 1st DECEMBER. 1857. ? i . The public meeting of planters and merchants advertised in our columns was held in this town on Friday last. On Mr. Auþÿnesen sbeing called to the chair, a full statement was given of the object of the meeting and of the questionspending, and a number of resolutions previousty agreed on by the gentlemen who had called the meeting, were read and discussed. The meeting adjourned to Monday, when after a new discussion the following resolutions were agreed to : þÿ Resolved, that with full acknowledgement of the right of the Danish legislative power to alter the present duties ! on colonial produce, as shall appear to them just anti proper, this meeting deprecates and protests against any j public act implying that the citizens ; of this colony are not entitled within j the extent of the Danjsh monarchy to the same regard, and the same, at least native protection of their industry, which is considered due or is practically granted to the inhabitants of the mother-country and of its other colo- i nies ; and the people of this Island hopes and demands, that neither fiscal theories, nor local or trades-intercsts will be taken by the government, the legislature, or the people of Denmark to warrant any act tending to deal with the agricultural produce of this Danish island al foreign produce, that , may be taxed exclusively with a view to realize the highest obtainable customs revenue therefrom. Resolved, that the small and long estab-

lished difference on the import duty to Denmark in favor of sugar the produce of the Danish islands, amounting to about fifty cents pr. 100 lb., ought ; not to be disturbed or reduced by any new fiscal relations. That difference being already a minimum, the fractional amounts thereof now proposed to be allowed for a few years, would ! not likely come to or be of appreciable j value to the producers. Resolved, that there is not known any precedent (if precedents were to furnish an excuse) for a proceeding like the one now in question in any modern J state towards its colonies. The once declared intention of the Bri- j tish government to assimilate the fo- j reign and colonial sugar duties, w-ould > even if carried out not constitute such j precedent ; the main motives for that j course being of no application to Denmark. Besides the British colonies had gone through the difficulties of emancipation much earlier, had been largely compensated and otherwise protected ; they have been powerfully assisted to obtain laborers, and are generally not called on to pay taxes to the British government, or to bear the expenses of government and military establishments ; þÿ our case being i as yet in most respects the reverse ' thereof. Our staple industry, which j has suffered and is suffering most se- I ' verely, is already taxed for state purposes far beyond what is known of any other colony in the Westindies. Resolved, that the proposition to assimilate the duty on foreign refined or half
refined sugars ground or otherwise pulverized with the duty on St. Croix Muscovadoes, only leaving for some

years a nominal difference (respectively about i and IjlOofacent pr. pound) on those very different classes of sugar, appears to be made more in favor of those using only refined sugar and of refiners, in Denmark than consistently with principles of fiscal- legislation, þÿ and that it appears most probable, that such an effactment, evidently tending to do away with the use of Muscovado sugar, would likely within a short time make it impossible to carry any St. Croix sugars to Denmark, except those of the lowest quality for the use of refiners. This meeting considers, that jf any such enactment were to pass, the present import duty on Danish West India sugars ought at once to be abolished, and those sugars admitted like any other danish produce free of duty. Resolved, that while those proposed new enactments would be unjust and ruinous to the colony, it would be but just to St. Croix, and also in the ligitimate interest of the public revenue, that the remnants of antiquated þÿ þÿColonial restrictions, hampering the trade of the Island, should be done away with ; and especially, that, even granting that the ordinary export duty of respectively 5 pr. cent and 3 pr. cent on sugar and rum be a fair taxation on cane estates, the double duty nowcharged thereon when exported to Thomas) orin vessels not þÿprivileged, other places than Denmark|(even to St. þÿ should be forthwith abolished. That the said double export duty is neither more nor less than a penalty imposed to prevent our produce from going to

other places than to Denmark, and that it lias been kept up not only to the manifest detriment of this Island, but also to the manifest detriment of State revenues, by forcing into tinhome market quantities of Colonial sugars to the exclusion from the market of corresponding quantities of foreign produce, that would have paid the higher duty ; an irregularity which it is now sought to compensate by denationalizing the produce of the colony. Resolved, that the above resolutions be embodied in an address to be prsented to His Excellency the Governor, respectfully requesting him to 'represent the matter thereof to the home government, and to support the fair interests of the Island by his own perfect knowledge of the case and of its bearings on the best interests of the Colony and indeed of every class of its inhabitants. And it was further resolved. That the resolutions adopted by this meeting be communicated to the Burgher Council, it being expected, that the Council will use every exertion to defend the legitimate interests of the Island, and also that Messrs. Arnesen, Ratcliffm G. J. Mudie, J. Elliott who had called the meeting and Mr. Newton be requested to have the address agreed on drawn up, signed by planters and merchants and presented to His Excellency the Governor; and to communicate with the Burgher Council. The proceedings then closed.

MR. CAMPION. An advertisement in our columns to-day announces the expected arrival of Mr. Campion, the famous Photographic Artist, by specftil request. The self-evident proofs which his likenesses showed of their superiority are too fresh in the mind of the public to require comment on our part ; but he comes this time with new improvements, as his pictures are now taken in a far superior style than when here last. We copy the following very flattering testimony to the superior qualities of Mr. þÿC. s pictures, from a Jamaica Paper, where it appears they have gained for him a name well worthy of the attention of the lovers of artistic excellence in this community. Jamaica, Kingston, Nov. 17, 1857 The advertisement of Mr. Campion, appearing in our columns today, is worthy of special notice, and we would call the attention of our readers to it. Mr. Campion announces this as his last week, and we believe it is positively so Those who wish to secure good likenesses ,of themselves had therefore better lose no time, hut visit the Gallery opposite þÿMichell s Drug Store as early as possible this week, where pictures are taken in any weather, clear or cloudy. The Ambrotype is a likeness superior, in many points, to Daguerreotypes, or others of the kind and one of the principal excellencies of the style which we may mention is the fact that the pictures in Ambrotype is seen easily in any light, and does not require to be shaded, or to be held in any particular manner, to he properly seen.
Mr. Campion is perfect master of the art, and we can confidently recommend our readers to visit him, either for the satisfaction of having a good picture, or of seeing some flue specimens of the art.

On the morning of the 23rd, two strong pursuing columns,

Nicholson, who about this time breathed his last, left Delhi. They consisted each of about 1,660 infantry, 500 cavalry, three troops of Horse Artillery, and 18 guns. One of these, under the command of Colonel Grcathed, crossed over to the West bank of the river, and took the direction of Allyghur, where it arrived on the 29th. Ou the 27th, they overtook the enemy at Bolundshuhur, where the Jhansi rebels, with their artillery, with a miscellaneous assemblage of insurgents, having taken up a strong position, made a stand. After a sharp engagement, they were entirely defeated, driven through the town, and pursued beyond it They were scattered in all directions, leaving two guns, two ammunition waggons, and a vast number of bullock carts, loaded with small arm ammunition, in our hands. About one hundred were left dead on the field, and multitudes of the wounded and dying were seen to be carried away with them. Our casualties amounted to about sixty. Captain Best, of the 8th Cavalry ; Lieutenant Sarel and Cornet Blair, of tho 9th Lancers ; and Lieutenant Edgeworth, of the 8th Foot, were all severely wounded. Captain Drysdale, of the 9th Lancers, was much hurt by his horse, when shot, rolling over him The fort of Malaghur, in front of the advancing force, was at this time occupied by the enemy in strength ; when about to have been evacuated, and was taken possession of without resistance. The other column, which left on the same date, moved down by the Western hank of

the river, towards Agra, and overtook the rebels at Muttra, on the 28th, when they were attacked and defeated with heavy slaughter. Delhi and the country around it are now perfectly tranquil, and though sickness is prevalent among the troops, it is infinitely less so than might, under thd circumstances, have been expected. Singularly enough nearly four weeks have passed since these events occurred, we are still without tho casualty list, and all that we know of details are the scraps picked up and strung together from fragments of letters,'written mostly at a distance from the scone of action. It can hardly be supposed that the authorities are not, long before this, in possession of a vast amount of information, which continues to he withheld from the public. But mystcry-mongering, a failure only of the weak, has become a disease amongst the authorities
